name: Dana Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Dana, 43. I left school after secondary school and learned saxophone in local bands, so I still sit in the junior chair at the civic dance orchestra. I record simple horn parts and teach beginners, and I like it when the whole section lands a rhythm together; reading a new score fast is still hard for me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do the work and household money fit together?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The orchestra contract and a few school sessions pay well for music work, and we have eight months of household expenses saved. My partner repairs buses; we have two children in school and a mortgage. There are many other music posts nearby, but I would have to audition or meet their teaching requirements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the orchestra that a quicker booking sheet is welcome, but we still have to rehearse the dance set. My beginners still need me to hear when a long note runs out of breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI now and then to tidy a practice sheet, and I check the notes against my horn. I worry more about the next audition than about a tiny software change, though the savings make an ordinary gap bearable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the junior chair, four beginner pupils and the two monthly recording calls this year. In the first year I’d move a fifth of each cleared recording fee into our mortgage reserve after the players and travel are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the household in this picture. Eight months of expenses gives us time to fix a missed booking without missing the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the reserve let your family do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The reserve means my partner and I can turn down a recording date that pays less than travel. It is money for a real break in work, not a new saxophone just because one is advertised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the job do you already use AI for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it for a first draft of exercises, not for deciding how a child sounds. I have never learned the score-checking feature; a senior player would need to show me before I trust it.

I would tell players that a live **dance set** still requires us to listen together.
think: My **eight-month reserve** cushions a missed recording call or audition gap.
I use AI **occasionally** for practice drafts and check the notes myself.
do: Keep the **junior chair**, four pupils and two monthly recording calls this year.
Save a **fifth of cleared fees** in the first year after player and travel costs.
feel: I feel **calm** about the mortgage with several months of expenses saved.

fieldNote: Her **higher pay** and reserve buffer normal gaps despite a junior chair and mortgage.
She uses AI for **draft exercises**, not a new score-checking skill in this scenario.

steps.text: Keep junior chair, four pupils and two monthly recording calls this year
Save fifth of cleared recording fees in first year after player and travel costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say generated horn parts could make small studio calls rarer, and I would ask the musicians’ association for clear session fees. The orchestra should not quietly add unpaid editing to a rehearsal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio calls are roughly a fifth of my music pay, and I am the easiest chair to leave off a recording. The family can absorb a short loss, but a permanent cut would shrink what we put aside for the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d learn the new AI score-checking feature with the senior player, testing it on parts I own before I use it at work. In the first year, if studio calls fall, I’d ask the association for a written session-fee meeting and cut the paid practice-room day rather than keep spending against missing fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own recording work despite the savings. Junior players rarely get the first studio call when a budget gets tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the first fee loss show up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first lost call would be a two-hour horn session that helps pay the school transport bill. I would record each cancelled date for three months before assuming the whole contract is ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the new tool change your junior standing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The feature might catch a wrong note before rehearsal, but it will not turn me into the section leader. I would keep checking its results with my own score until it earns my trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my family that thinking AGI by 2028 could take written parts and lesson plans before capable robots play horns around 2031. A three-year wait for robots does not keep the studio phone ringing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The recording calls and some beginner planning could go quickly, and I could be next when the orchestra needs fewer players. Eight months of savings helps, but the mortgage and two children make a long gap serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d ask the orchestra for written paid dates and list how much comes from studio work. In the first year after AGI arrives, if calls stop, I’d drop the outside practice-room rental, apply for a posted school music-aide vacancy only if the school confirms I qualify with my present schooling and the wage covers travel and my mortgage share, and keep the orchestra chair until a real offer comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, not frozen. I know several schools nearby, but I would check the posted qualifications and wage before treating an opening as an option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your pay changes in 2028 before robot players?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The score preparation can vanish in 2028; live horn work faces another deadline around 2031. If the orchestra also cuts my chair, that is when the reserve starts going down each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your partner carry the mortgage during a search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner’s bus workshop wage covers part of the mortgage, not the whole household. We would show the children a quieter holiday plan, but I would not ask them to solve an adult bill.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from capable robot players around 2031.
I would tell my family that live horns have a **later deadline** than studio planning.
think: Studio calls and beginner planning could **disappear quickly**.
Our **mortgage and children** make a long gap serious despite savings.
do: Get written **orchestra dates** and list studio pay before 2028; keep the chair until a real offer.
Drop outside **practice-room rent** in first year after 2028 if calls stop.
Apply for **posted aide work** after 2028 only if calls stop, school confirms eligibility and pay covers travel and mortgage share.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible studio and orchestra losses while I can still act.
S2.quote: A three-year wait for robots does not keep the studio phone ringing.
fieldNote: She expects **thinking work** to weaken in 2028 before robot horns arrive around 2031.
Her **school search** needs a posted vacancy, confirmed eligibility and adequate wage; she holds paid orchestra work until an offer.

steps.text: Confirm paid orchestra dates and list studio income before 2028
Drop outside practice-room rent in first year after 2028 if studio calls stop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years lets us ask schools what paid teaching really requires before paying for certificates. Thinking AGI arrives by 2031, while capable robots for live playing follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could become a stronger beginner teacher if I practise and observe a good one. I cannot assume a school will hire a secondary-school graduate just because I have played paid dances for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This term I’d ask two schools whether a short teaching certificate qualifies me for their posted music-aide roles. I’d take the course only if a school accepts it and a grant pays tuition. Classes must miss no paid orchestra dates, and my partner must be able to cover school pickup. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for an open role if recording pay falls and I have the required certificate, while keeping paid pupils until offered work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the studio part, but I can plan without risking the mortgage on tuition. The extra time matters only if a school tells me what it will pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a certificate actually qualify you for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the job description and the certificate name in writing. A course that sounds useful but is not accepted for a paid post is not worth our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the training grant is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the grant is refused, I would keep the orchestra and pupils while checking another local vacancy. I would not borrow from the mortgage reserve to buy a certificate that may never pay back.

I would place **2031 thinking AGI** before robot horn players around 2034.
think: A short **teaching certificate** could help only if a school accepts it.

do: Check **school job requirements** this term; seek another local vacancy if the training grant fails.

S3.quote: A course that sounds useful but is not accepted for a paid post is not worth our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the children that music and steady paid work can go together if we keep learning. Thinking AGI in 2036 and robots that can play around 2039 leave a decade, but we still need written fees today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I could have more pupils, though I cannot count on them now. Our mortgage will not be gone just because the forecast is slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep the paid orchestra dates and pupils and save a fifth of cleared recording fees after essentials. Over the decade I’d take the teaching certificate only if a school confirms it qualifies me for a paid post and a grant pays tuition without missed orchestra work and my partner can cover pickup; in the first year after 2036 I’d keep paid lessons and apply for an open school role if studio income falls and I have earned any required certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about what live bands earn at the far end, but our pay looks solid now. Eight months saved means I can take a careful route instead of buying a course tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do during the decade, rather than at its end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the association to keep a written list of session rates and recording reuse terms each year. That gives a junior player something to show when a new studio offers less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children depend on music for their future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children to finish school and learn what they enjoy, then ask what each job pays. I would not make them carry the mortgage worry into their own choices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because studio calls could stop while my junior chair is also exposed. Written orchestra dates, a posted music-aide role with a living wage and a funded certificate that schools accept would help. I can use savings for a gap, not for a course that gives no paid work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets a first chance when a studio has fewer sessions. A junior horn player needs a written rate as much as the section leader does.

portrait: Dana is a **43-year-old junior saxophonist** with secondary schooling, teaching four beginners and playing a civic dance orchestra.
Her **higher pay** and eight-month reserve support a mortgage and two children, while nearby posts still require auditions or qualifications.
She uses **AI occasionally**, learning a new score checker only with a senior player and owned parts.
Fast AGI threatens **studio calls** before robot horns; she checks school requirements and funding before training.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could end junior recording calls while orchestra seats also face cuts.
whatWouldHelp: Written **orchestra dates** and a posted music-aide job at a living wage would support a transition.
A **funded certificate** that schools accept would let her study without losing paid work.
